problemText: Every object that has mass exerts a pull on every other object that has mass. What is the name of this pull?
choices: Gravity
Magnetism
Friction
Momentum
hints: This pull acts between any two objects with mass, no matter how far apart they are.
This is the force that keeps planets in orbit around the sun.

problemText: A rock is thrown hard across a frozen lake with no friction. If no forces acted on the rock, which path would it follow? Now explain why the rock does not actually follow that path.
choices: It would fly off in a straight line because it is moving fast; the cold temperature causes it to curve downward.
It would fly off in a straight line because there is nothing to change its direction; gravity pulls it downward and curves its path instead.
It would circle around the lake because the ice pushes it sideways; gravity has no effect on objects moving across ice because they are sliding on a cold surface.
It would slow down and stop because all moving objects eventually stop unless pushed; gravity pulls it upward and prevents it from sinking into the frozen lake.
hints: Think about what happens to any moving object if nothing pushes or pulls on it.
Gravity always acts on the rock, whether it is in the air or on the ice—it never switches off.

problemText: A spacecraft is in orbit around Earth. Inside the spacecraft, an astronaut releases a pencil and watches it float in the air rather than drop to the floor. What does this tell you about whether Earth's gravity is still pulling on the pencil?
choices: Gravity is pulling on Earth but not on the pencil, because the pencil is made of lighter material and does not experience gravitational force.
Gravity is no longer pulling on the pencil, because objects in orbit escape Earth's gravitational pull completely when they reach orbital altitude.
Gravity is still pulling on the pencil, because the pencil and the astronaut are both falling toward Earth at the same rate.
Gravity is pulling downward on the pencil, which is why it appears to float upward away from the floor because the downward pull is stronger than the floor.
hints: Remember that gravity does not switch off in space—it keeps pulling the entire time an object orbits.
An orbiting spacecraft and everything inside it are all in free fall together toward Earth.

problemText: Two satellites have identical mass and are both in stable orbit around Earth. Satellite P orbits very close to Earth, while Satellite Q orbits much farther away. Both satellites are moving fast enough to stay in orbit. Which satellite feels the stronger pull of Earth's gravity, and what would happen to Satellite Q if it were suddenly slowed down to half its current speed?
choices: Satellite Q feels the stronger pull because the farther an object is from Earth, the stronger the gravitational attraction becomes; Satellite Q would immediately crash into Earth because gravity overcomes its velocity.

Satellite Q feels the stronger pull because it has traveled a greater total distance from Earth's center over time; Satellite Q would fly off into space because slowing it down reduces the strength of gravity's pull on it.

Satellite P feels the stronger pull because it orbits faster and experiences more gravitational force; Satellite Q would continue to orbit at the same distance because gravity always holds satellites in place no matter their speed.
Satellite P feels the stronger pull because it is closer to Earth; Satellite Q would fall toward Earth instead of orbiting because slower sideways motion means it cannot keep missing the ground.
hints: Gravity's pull grows weaker as distance increases—which satellite is closer?
An orbit requires the right balance between falling toward the central body and moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.

problemText: A moon orbits Planet A at a distance of 100,000 kilometers. An identical moon orbits Planet B at the exact same distance. Planet B is far more massive than Planet A. Explain why the moon orbiting Planet B feels a stronger gravitational pull, and describe what would need to change for the moon around Planet A to feel an equally strong pull from its planet.
choices: Planet B pulls more strongly because it is more massive; the moon around Planet A would need to orbit much closer to its planet to feel an equally strong pull.
Planet B pulls more strongly because it is farther from the sun; the moon around Planet A would need to move much faster to feel an equally strong pull.
Planet A pulls more strongly because smaller planets have denser material; the moon around Planet B would need to be moved farther away to balance the pull.
Planet B pulls more strongly because larger planets rotate faster; the moon around Planet A would need to have more mass to match the pull it receives.
hints: A more massive object pulls more strongly than a less massive one—which planet is more massive?
Distance and mass are the two factors that determine how strong a gravitational pull is; changing distance is one way to change how strong a pull feels.

problemText: A ball rolls off a table and hits the ground a few meters away. A satellite is launched into orbit and circles Earth repeatedly for years without ever hitting the ground, even though Earth's gravity is pulling on both the ball and the satellite the entire time. Both gravity and the path each object follows are outcomes of the same rule. Explain what is different between the ball and the satellite, why that difference matters, and how gravity's pull on each object produces such different results.
choices: The ball falls because gravity is pulling on it, while the satellite orbits because gravity switches off once it is far enough from Earth; gravity only works on objects close to the ground where its force is concentrated.

The ball has very little sideways speed when gravity starts acting on it, so gravity pulls it straight down to the ground quickly; the satellite has enormous sideways speed, so gravity curves its path around Earth instead of down, allowing it to keep falling and also keep missing the ground over and over.

The ball is moving slowly sideways when it leaves the table, so gravity pulls it down faster than it can travel forward and it strikes the ground; the satellite moves forward at tremendous speed, which means gravity bends its path into a circle while the satellite continues moving and misses Earth repeatedly.

The ball falls because the pull of gravity on it is directed straight downward with no sideways motion to counteract it; the satellite orbits because its velocity in the forward direction balances the inward pull of gravity, creating a curved path that repeatedly brings it close to Earth without collision.
hints: Both the ball and satellite are pulled toward Earth by gravity—the key difference is how fast each is moving sideways when that pull starts acting on it.
An orbit happens when an object is pulled toward a central body and also moves sideways fast enough to keep missing it; think about what 'sideways speed' means for each object.

problemText: The sun's real diameter is about 1,392,000 kilometers, and Earth's real diameter is about 12,742 kilometers. Which statement correctly describes the size relationship between these two objects?
choices: Earth's diameter is about 109 times larger than the sun's diameter
About 109 suns lined up edge to edge would stretch across Earth's diameter
About 109 Earths lined up edge to edge would stretch across the sun's diameter
The sun and Earth are almost the same size, just a few kilometers apart
hints: Try dividing the sun's diameter by Earth's diameter to find how many times larger the sun is.
Remember that when one number is much bigger than another, it takes many copies of the smaller one to equal the larger one.

problemText: A student builds a scale model of the solar system using a 30-centimeter beach ball to represent the sun. The sun's real diameter is about 1,392,000 kilometers. If every centimeter in this model stands for about 46,400 real kilometers, what real distance does a model distance of 2 centimeters represent?
choices: About 46,400 kilometers
About 23,200 kilometers
About 184,000 kilometers
About 92,800 kilometers
hints: Multiply the model distance by the scale factor to find the real distance.
The scale factor tells you how many real kilometers are represented by each model centimeter.

problemText: Jupiter's real diameter is about 139,820 kilometers, and Earth's real diameter is about 12,742 kilometers. In a scale model where Earth is represented by a small marble about 1 centimeter across, about how big should Jupiter be in this same model?
choices: About 11 centimeters across
About 1 centimeter across
About 0.1 centimeters across
About 100 centimeters across
hints: Find the ratio by dividing Jupiter's real diameter by Earth's real diameter.
If Earth is 1 centimeter in the model, multiply that by the ratio you just found to get Jupiter's model size.

problemText: In a scale model with a 30-centimeter beach ball representing the sun, Earth's model size works out to about 2.7 millimeters (like a sesame seed) and Earth's model distance from the ball is about 32 meters. If you were to include Mars in the same model, and Mars's real distance from the sun is about 1.5 times Earth's real distance, why would Mars sit much farther from the ball than it is from the beach ball in terms of size, even though Mars itself is only slightly more distant than Earth?
choices: Mars is actually smaller than Earth, so its model representation must be even tinier than Earth's, making it appear insignificant relative to the beach ball sun despite being farther away

The same scale factor applies to both size and distance, but distances are so much larger in reality that even small ratio differences create huge model differences, while planetary sizes are so small that they all appear tiny in the model

The scale factor used for planetary diameters is much smaller than the scale factor used for orbital distances, which causes Mars to appear much farther from the sun than its actual size would suggest in a single unified model

The sun's enormous size in the model forces all planets to be placed at distances proportional to their real distances, but since planetary sizes shrink when divided by the scale factor, Mars ends up looking far from the sun even though it is only slightly larger than Earth
hints: Think about whether Earth's model distance (32 meters) or Earth's model size (2.7 millimeters) is the bigger number.
Real distances in the solar system are much, much larger than real planetary diameters, even though they use the same scale factor.

problemText: A student knows that Mars sits at about 1.5 AU (astronomical units) from the sun, and Jupiter sits at about 5.2 AU from the sun. Earth sits at 1 AU. In a scale model where Earth's distance from the model sun is marked at 10 meters, where should the student mark Mars and Jupiter's positions if they use the same scale factor for all distances?
choices: Mars at about 52 meters and Jupiter at about 15 meters from the model sun
Mars at about 5 meters and Jupiter at about 2 meters from the model sun
Mars at about 15 meters and Jupiter at about 52 meters from the model sun
Mars at about 1.5 meters and Jupiter at about 5.2 meters from the model sun
hints: Each planet's distance from the sun in the model should be multiplied by the same factor used for Earth's distance.
If Earth at 1 AU is 10 meters in the model, then a distance of 1.5 AU should be 1.5 times as far as Earth, and 5.2 AU should be 5.2 times as far.

problemText: A student creates a scale model with a basketball (about 24 centimeters across) representing the sun. Another student creates a scale model with a 30-centimeter beach ball representing the sun. Both students want Earth to be shown at the correct relative size in their models. Will Earth be the same size in both models, smaller in the basketball model, or larger in the basketball model? Explain your reasoning using what you know about how scale factors work.
choices: Earth will be larger in the basketball model because the basketball is smaller than the beach ball, so the scale factor is larger, and when Earth's real diameter is divided by a smaller scale factor, the result is a larger model size
Earth will be the same size in both models because Earth's real diameter never changes, no matter which object represents the sun

Earth will be larger in the basketball model because a smaller object representing the sun means planets must be larger to maintain the correct ratio of planetary size to sun size in the visual representation
Earth will be smaller in the basketball model because the basketball is smaller than the beach ball, so the scale factor is larger, making everything smaller when divided by it
hints: Remember that the scale factor is the real size of the sun divided by the model size of the sun (the ball).
A smaller ball chosen to represent the sun creates a larger scale factor, which means when you divide Earth's real diameter by that larger number, you get a smaller result.

problemText: A small rock fragment is currently traveling through space, far from Earth and not inside any planet's atmosphere. What is this object called?
choices: Meteor
Meteoroid
Meteorite
Asteroid
hints: Think about what location the object is in right now.
The name changes based on where the object is, not what it is made of.

problemText: An object in the solar system is made of rock and metal. It orbits the sun in a path that stays roughly the same distance from the sun all the way around. Where would you expect to find most objects like this one?
choices: In the Kuiper Belt, far beyond Neptune
In a long, stretched-out orbit that swings far from the sun and close to it
In the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter
Orbiting as a moon around one of the outer planets
hints: Rocky, metallic composition is a clue to which type of object this is.
The asteroid belt is located between which two planets?

problemText: A glowing streak of light flashes across Earth's night sky. A person watching calls it a shooting star. What is this streak of light actually called in scientific terms?
choices: A meteorite that has already landed on Earth's surface after passing through the atmosphere
A comet's tail pointing away from the sun due to solar wind and radiation pressure
A meteoroid still traveling through space before it enters Earth's atmosphere and begins to burn
A meteor produced by a burning fragment in the atmosphere
hints: The term changes based on where the object is — this one is in Earth's atmosphere.
Which stage happens when friction heats a fragment until it glows in the sky?

problemText: A scientist observes a solar system object that is round in shape because its own gravity pulled it into that round form. The object orbits the sun in the region between Mars and Jupiter. However, many other rocky objects of similar size orbit in the same region, and this object has not pushed them out or cleared them away. Is this object a dwarf planet, an asteroid, or a comet? Explain your reasoning using at least two facts about the object.
choices: A dwarf planet, because it is round from its own gravity but has not cleared other objects out of its orbital neighborhood
An asteroid, because it orbits between Mars and Jupiter in the asteroid belt region where large rocky bodies are always found together
A comet, because it is round in shape and orbits the sun like all other bodies in the solar system do
A dwarf planet, because it has strong enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape, which is the defining feature of any dwarf planet
hints: What is the key difference between a dwarf planet and a full planet — or between a dwarf planet and an asteroid?
Two clues point to the answer: the object is round, AND it shares its orbital neighborhood with similar-sized debris.

problemText: A comet travels through space on a long, stretched-out orbit. Right now it is far from the sun, moving outward into the cold reaches of the outer solar system. As it moves, a glowing tail streams behind it. In which direction is this tail actually pointing, and why?
choices: Backward along the direction the comet is moving, because material naturally trails behind any object as it travels through space
Away from the sun, even though the comet is moving away from the sun, so the tail actually points in front of the comet
Toward the sun, pulled by the sun's strong gravitational force on the comet's ices and gases
In a curved path that follows the comet's orbit around the sun, staying aligned with its trajectory
hints: What causes a comet's tail to form — is it the comet's motion or the sun's heat?
When the comet is moving away from the sun, where does the sun lie in relation to the comet?

problemText: A pea-sized rock fragment has been drifting through space for millions of years. One night it enters Earth's atmosphere at high speed, and friction heats it until it produces a bright streak across the sky. An observer on the ground sees this streak and exclaims, 'Look, a shooting star!' About half of the fragment burns up as it falls through the atmosphere, but the remaining pieces hit the ground in a field. A geologist collects one of these pieces the next morning. Name what this object was called at each of the three stages — while it drifted in space, while it burned in the atmosphere producing the streak of light, and after it landed on the ground. Then explain why the same piece of rock has three different names.
choices: Asteroid, then meteor, then meteorite; the three names describe different objects formed as the rock breaks apart
Meteoroid, then comet, then asteroid; the names change based on how much of the object survives each stage
Meteoroid, then meteor, then meteorite; the three names describe the same object at different locations, not three different objects
Space rock, then falling rock, then ground rock; the names are informal ways of describing the object's speed and position
hints: Is the object the same piece throughout, or does it turn into a different kind of thing at each stage?
What is the rule for when names change — is it based on what the object is made of, or where it is located?

problemText: Which of these four planets is a terrestrial planet?
choices: Neptune
Jupiter
Saturn
Venus
hints: Terrestrial planets are small and rocky.
Think about which planets orbit close to the sun, before the asteroid belt.

problemText: A scientist discovers a planet that is very large, made mostly of gases, and has no solid surface anywhere. Where in the solar system would you expect this planet to orbit?
choices: Beyond the asteroid belt
Between Earth and Mars
Between Mercury and Venus
Closer to the sun than Mercury
hints: Gas and ice giants share a location pattern in the solar system.
The asteroid belt marks where a major group boundary occurs.

problemText: Saturn is famous for its bright, easy-to-see ring system. Which statement correctly explains what this tells you about Saturn's classification?
choices: Saturn is a terrestrial planet because it has rings that distinguish it from all other planets in the solar system.
Saturn is a giant planet because all giant planets have ring systems, even though only Saturn's rings are easy to see.
Saturn is a terrestrial planet because its rings prove it orbits close to the sun like Earth and Venus do.
Saturn is a dwarf planet because its visible rings indicate it is smaller than the other giant planets.
hints: Remember that all four giant planets have rings, not just Saturn.
The brightness of Saturn's rings tells you something different than the fact that it has rings.

problemText: A newly observed planet has these properties: it is small, it has a solid rocky surface, and it has no ring system. A student claims this is not enough information to sort it into a group because the planet's exact distance from the sun in kilometers is unknown. What is the best response to this claim?
choices: The student is correct; without knowing the exact distance in kilometers, you cannot determine whether the planet is terrestrial or giant.
The student is correct; both terrestrial and giant planets can have small sizes and rocky surfaces, so distance from the sun must be measured precisely to classify any planet correctly.
The student is wrong; the small size, rocky composition, and lack of rings already match the terrestrial pattern, and those properties together are enough to sort it.
The student is wrong; distance from the sun matters less than checking whether a planet has a solid surface, and this one does, which proves it must be terrestrial.
hints: Multiple different types of clues about composition, structure, and features can agree on one answer.
Knowing which side of the asteroid belt a planet orbits is helpful, but is that the only information you have here?

problemText: Two planets are being classified. Planet A is much larger than Earth, made mostly of gas, has no solid surface, and orbits far beyond the asteroid belt. Planet B is small, rocky, has a solid surface, and orbits close to the sun. A student says both planets should be classified the same way because both are planets. Why is this student's reasoning incorrect?
choices: Planets are only classified into groups if they are larger than Jupiter, and Planet B does not meet this size requirement.
Planet classification depends on whether a planet is visible from Earth without a telescope, and this information is not provided for either world.
Only planets with ring systems can be placed into classification groups, and one of these planets has no rings.
The two planets have opposite properties in composition, size, surface, and location, so they belong in different groups.
hints: Look at the properties listed for each planet and compare them to the patterns of terrestrial and giant planets.
One planet fits every property of the gas/ice giant group while the other fits every property of the terrestrial group.

problemText: A student reads that Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune all have ring systems and all orbit beyond the asteroid belt. The student then argues, 'Size is what really decides whether a planet is a giant, because Jupiter and Saturn are bigger than Uranus and Neptune, yet all four are classified the same way.' Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and explain what actually determines the classification.
choices: The student mistook a supporting detail for the real reason; all four planets are giants because they are much larger than any terrestrial planet, are made mostly of gas and ice, and have no solid surface—not because of size differences among themselves.

The student's comparison is invalid because it ignores that all four planets share the same composition of gases and liquids with no solid ground, which is the actual feature that defines the giant planet group.
The student is correct; the four giant planets have no other properties in common besides their location beyond the asteroid belt, so size differences are the only way to tell them apart.

The student's reasoning is flawed because it focuses on differences between giant planets; instead, the classification is based on how all giant planets differ together from terrestrial planets in composition, structure, and atmosphere.
hints: A property that every planet in a group shares is what matters for the classification, not differences within the group.
What are all four of those planets made of, and what would happen if you tried to land a spacecraft on one?
